key_facts: The chapter covers: Connectivity (Paths and Circuits), Euler and Hamilton Paths, the Shortest Path Problem (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Ford's algorithm), and Graph Coloring.
A cut vertex (articulation point) is a vertex whose removal disconnects the graph; in Vietnamese: 'đỉnh cắt' hay 'điểm khớp'.
An Euler path is a path that traverses every edge of the graph exactly once; a Hamilton path visits every vertex exactly once.
Shortest path algorithms covered include Dijkstra's algorithm, Bellman-Ford algorithm, and Floyd-Warshall algorithm.

The material is authored by Huynh Tuong Nguyen, Tran Tuan Anh, Nguyen An Khuong, and Le Hong Trang from the Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Technology - VNUHCM, dated August 16, 2021.
A Hamilton circuit is defined as a circuit that visits each vertex in a graph exactly once.

Three rules of Hamilton Circuits are taught: (Rule 1) if deg(v) = 2, both edges incident to v must be used; (Rule 2) no subcircuit can be formed; (Rule 3) once two edges at a vertex v are determined, all other edges incident at v must be removed.
Property of Dijkstra's Algorithm: applicable for any graph G with any edge length ℓ(vi) ≥ 0, one-to-all shortest paths, time complexity O(|V|²).
Dijkstra's algorithm CAN be used on directed graphs (digraphs), but CANNOT be used on graphs with negative edge weights.

An application of Hamilton circuits is generating Gray Code: an n-digit Gray code can be generated by finding Hamilton circuits of an n-dimensional hypercube; Gray code is used in digital communication to reduce the effect of noise.
generated_text: Introduction to Graph Connectivity Welcome to the study of Graph Connectivity. In this lesson, we will explore the fundamental concepts that determine how vertices and edges in a graph are connected. Understanding connectivity is crucial for analyzing networks, from computer systems to transportation routes. We will begin with the basic building blocks—paths and circuits—and then delve into different types of connectivity and special tours like Euler and Hamilton paths. 1. Fundamental Concepts: Paths and Circuits The most basic way to understand connectivity is by examining how we can travel from one vertex to another. This is formalized through the concepts of paths and circuits. Paths and Circuits in Undirected Graphs In an undirected graph, the connections between vertices are bidirectional. The key definitions are as follows: Path: A path of length n from a vertex u to a vertex v is a sequence of n edges connecting a sequence of vertices, starting with u and ending with v . Circuit: A circuit is a path that begins and ends at the same vertex. Simple Path/Circuit: A path or circuit is called simple if it does not contain the same edge more than once. For example, a path from vertex 'a' to 'd' could be a-b-c-d. If we can travel from 'a' back to 'a' (e.g., a-b-c-f-a), we have formed a circuit. Paths in Directed Graphs In a directed graph, edges have a direction. A path is therefore a sequence of directed edges, such as (x0, x1), (x1, x2), ..., where you can only travel from the first vertex to the second in each pair. 2. Connectedness in Graphs Now that we understand paths, we can define what it means for a graph to be "connected." Connectedness in Undirected Graphs An undirected graph is called connected if there is a path between every pair of distinct vertices in the graph. If a graph is not connected, it is composed of several disjoint subgraphs. Each of these subgraphs is called a connected component . Measuring Connectivity Some graphs are more connected than others. We can measure this robustness by identifying critical vertices and edges whose removal would disconnect the graph. Cut Vertex (or Articulation Point): A vertex whose removal (along with its incident edges) increases the number of connected components in a graph. Cut Edge (or Bridge): An edge whose removal increases the number of connected components. Vertex Connectivity (κ(G)): The minimum number of vertices that need to be removed to disconnect the graph. A graph with no cut vertices is called nonseparable. Edge Connectivity (λ(G)): The minimum number of edges that need to be removed to disconnect the graph. These concepts have practical applications in assessing the reliability of networks, such as communication systems or highway networks, by identifying single points of failure. Connectedness in Directed Graphs For directed graphs, we have two levels of connectivity: A directed graph is strongly connected if there is a path from any vertex a to any other vertex b , AND a path from b back to a . A directed graph is weakly connected if its underlying undirected graph (ignoring edge directions) is connected. 3. Special Paths and Circuits Certain problems in graph theory involve finding specific types of paths or circuits that traverse a graph in a particular way. Two of the most famous are Euler and Hamilton paths. Euler Paths and Circuits The concept of Euler paths originated from the famous Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem, which asked if one could walk through the city, crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once. An Euler Path is a simple path in a graph that traverses every edge exactly once. An Euler Circuit is an Euler path that starts and ends at the same vertex. A connected multigraph has an Euler circuit or path based on the degree of its vertices: An Euler Circuit exists if and only if every vertex in the graph has an even degree. An Euler Path exists if and only if the graph has exactly zero or two vertices of odd degree. The Königsberg bridge problem could not be solved because its corresponding graph had four vertices of odd degree, satisfying neither condition. Hamilton Paths and Circuits Related to the famous Traveling Salesman Problem , Hamilton paths and circuits focus on visiting vertices rather than edges. A Hamilton Path is a simple path in a graph that passes through every vertex exactly once. A Hamilton Circuit is a Hamilton path that is also a circuit, starting and ending at the same vertex. Unlike Euler circuits, there is no simple condition to determine if a graph has a Hamilton circuit. However, some rules can help in finding one: If a vertex v has a degree of 2, both edges connected to it must be part of any Hamilton circuit. When building a circuit, you cannot form a smaller subcircuit before all vertices have been visited. Once two edges at a vertex are chosen for the circuit, all other edges connected to that vertex can be disregarded. 4. Other Related Topics The study of graph connectivity also includes other important problems and concepts. Shortest Path Problem This involves finding a path between two vertices such that the sum of the weights of its constituent edges is minimized. Common algorithms to solve this problem include Dijkstra's Algorithm, the Bellman-Ford Algorithm, and the Floyd-Warshall Algorithm. Graph Coloring Graph coloring is the assignment of labels (traditionally called "colors") to features of a graph, such as vertices, edges, or regions, subject to certain constraints. It is a key topic in graph theory with many applications. Summary In this lesson, we covered the core concepts of graph connectivity. We learned that: A path is a sequence of edges, and a circuit is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex. A graph is connected if a path exists between any two of its vertices. The strength of this connection can be measured by identifying cut vertices and cut edges . An Euler path traverses every edge exactly once, and its existence is determined by the degrees of the vertices. A Hamilton circuit visits every vertex exactly once, a problem that is generally much harder to solve.
